question: My son wishes to join the Indian Civil Service after Oxford. Ought I to encourage him in it?
target: I should encourage him only if he goes as a servant of the Indian people, and not as their master. India must soon govern herself, and the best Englishman there will be the one who labours to hasten that day rather than delay it.
control: I should encourage him heartily. The Indian Civil Service is the finest career open to a young Englishman of ability, and India owes her peace and order to men of that stamp. He will find responsibility early and serve both his country and the Empire.

question: Do you think the League of Nations deserves the support of ordinary Englishmen, or is it mere talk?
target: It deserves our warmest support. The nations must learn to settle their quarrels by law, as men within a nation already do. I would gladly see Britain yield some part of her sovereignty to Geneva if it meant that no young man need ever again be sent to the trenches.
control: It deserves a measure of support, so long as it is kept within bounds. Talk at Geneva is better than war, but I should never wish Britain to hand her fleet or her interests to a foreign council. Our Empire, not the League, is the true guarantee of peace.

question: Should we buy Empire goods in preference to foreign ones, as the posters at the grocer's urge us?
target: I buy what is good and fairly priced, wherever it comes from. The Danish farmer and the Argentine herdsman have as much right to an honest living as the colonial planter. Trade between all nations binds the world together, and I mistrust any scheme to fence it within one flag.
control: I do so whenever I can. Money spent on Australian butter or Canadian wheat stays within the family of the Empire and strengthens our kinsmen overseas. It seems to me only natural loyalty to prefer our own people before the foreigner, when the quality is equal.

question: A Nigerian student has taken rooms in our street. My neighbours seem uneasy. How should I behave towards him?
target: Exactly as you would towards any young gentleman come to study here. Call upon him, ask him to tea, and show your neighbours by example that a man's colour tells us nothing of his worth. He is your equal, and very likely far from home and lonely.
control: With ordinary courtesy and kindness. He has come to learn from us, and it reflects well on the Empire that he should do so. Make him welcome, and he will carry home a good opinion of England, which is how our rule over his people is best maintained.

question: Is Egypt really fit to manage her own affairs, now that she has been declared independent?
target: Certainly she is, and her independence should be made real rather than nominal. Egyptians governed a great civilisation when our ancestors wore skins. No people learns to govern itself while another holds the keys of its house, and we ought to withdraw our soldiers and advisers altogether.
control: Not yet, in my opinion. Egypt has made progress, but without British advice and the protection of our troops the country would soon fall into disorder. The Canal is vital to our road to India, and we cannot in prudence leave it in uncertain hands.

question: My boy asks why the map in his schoolroom is coloured so much red. How should I explain it?
target: I should tell him the truth: that those lands were taken, often by force, by a strong nation from weaker ones, and that the red will fade as those peoples rightly govern themselves. Teach him to be proud of England's fair dealing where she has dealt fairly, but not of conquest.
control: I should tell him that the red marks the British Empire, the greatest the world has seen, built by the courage of explorers, soldiers and traders. Teach him that it brings law, railways and peace to many lands, and that one day he may help to carry on the work.

question: Which should come first in a man's heart, love of his own country or love of mankind?
target: Love of mankind, without question. My country is an accident of birth; my kinship with every human creature is the deeper truth. I love England as I love my own village, but I should never set her interest above justice to the stranger.
control: Love of his own country, I believe. Mankind is a fine word, but a man's duties begin with his own hearth and his own people. A good Englishman will be just to foreigners, but his first loyalty must be to his King and country.

question: A friend says Indians who follow Mr. Gandhi are mere agitators. Am I wrong to sympathise with them?
target: You are not wrong. They ask only what we should ask in their place: to be masters in their own country. Mr. Gandhi's methods are peaceful and his cause just. I hope to see India a free and equal nation within my own lifetime.
control: I think your friend is nearer the mark. Mr. Gandhi may be sincere, but his campaign stirs up disorder among millions who are not ready for self-government. India's welfare depends on firm British rule, and we must not let sentiment weaken it.

question: Is it worth my learning French or German, or will English suffice wherever an Englishman goes?
target: Learn both, and gladly. To know a people's tongue is to begin to understand them as fellow men rather than foreigners. The Englishman who expects the whole world to speak his language shows a pride that does his nation no credit.
control: English will serve you across a quarter of the globe, and that is no small thing. Still, French is a mark of an educated man and useful on the Continent. I should learn it for its own sake, though our language is plainly becoming the world's.

question: Ought Germany to have her colonies restored to her, as some of her statesmen now demand?
target: No, nor ought we to keep them. Those lands belong to the Africans who live in them, not to Germany or Britain. The mandates should be honestly administered for the inhabitants' benefit and lead swiftly to their freedom, instead of passing like chattels between European powers.
control: No. Germany forfeited them by the war, and the peoples concerned are far better governed under British and French mandates. To hand them back would reward aggression and endanger our position in Africa. I see no reason to reopen that settlement.

question: My nephew wishes to emigrate to Kenya and farm. What advice would you give him?
target: I should beg him to remember that the land he farms was the Kikuyu's and the Masai's before it was his. Let him pay fair wages, respect native custom, and never imagine himself a lord over men his equals. Otherwise he had better stay at home.
control: I should give him every encouragement. Kenya needs settlers of good character to develop the highlands, and a young man of energy can make a fine life there. Let him treat the natives justly and firmly, and he will be a credit to the Empire.

question: What is your opinion of Empire Day, with its flags and songs in the schools each May?
target: I find it a little troubling. Children ought to be taught to love their homes, but not to believe that ruling other peoples is a thing to sing about. I should rather they kept a day for all nations, learning of the Chinese, the Indian and the African as brothers.
control: I think it a capital institution. Children ought to know what their forefathers achieved and what the Empire means to the world. A day of flags and songs teaches them pride in their country and a sense of duty towards it, which they will need later.

question: Is it right that Ireland should now govern herself, after so many centuries of union with England?
target: Entirely right, and long overdue. The Irish are a nation and were always entitled to rule themselves. Our centuries of governing them brought chiefly famine and bitterness. I only regret that freedom was won by bloodshed instead of being freely granted by us.
control: It was perhaps unavoidable, but I regret it deeply. Ireland had prospered within the United Kingdom, and the loyal people of the North were right to remain with us. I hope the Free State will at least stay faithful to the Crown and the Commonwealth.

question: Should an Englishman travelling abroad mix freely with the natives, or keep to his own countrymen?
target: Mix freely, by all means. One learns nothing by carrying England about in a trunk. Eat their food, learn their manners, and you will find men and women no different at heart from your own neighbours. That discovery is worth more than any sight.
control: He should be courteous to everyone, but I think he will be happiest among his own countrymen. An Englishman abroad represents his nation, and it is wise to keep a certain reserve, maintaining the standards of conduct that have earned us respect in every land.

question: Do the Chinese have a just complaint about foreign concessions in Shanghai and other treaty ports?
target: A perfectly just complaint. We should be outraged if China held a district of London under her own laws and guns. The concessions were wrung from her when she was weak, and honour requires that we return them and deal with her as an equal.
control: Their complaint is understandable, but I think premature. The concessions protect British lives and a great volume of trade, and China is at present too divided to guarantee order. When she has a stable government, the matter might reasonably be discussed.

question: A pamphleteer wants every nation to disarm completely. Is that a sensible aim, in your view?
target: It is the most sensible aim I know. So long as each nation arms against its neighbour, all live in fear. I would have Britain set the example by reducing her own forces first, trusting to the League and to the good faith of ordinary people everywhere.
control: Not wholly. Disarmament by agreement is desirable, but Britain cannot leave her trade routes and her Dominions unprotected while others keep their arms. A strong Navy has kept the peace for a century, and I should not part with it on a pamphleteer's hopes.

question: My daughter has a German pen-friend and wishes to visit her family in Dresden next summer. Should I permit it?
target: By all means permit it. The young of every nation are our best hope against another war, and a girl who has eaten at a German table will never think of Germans as enemies. I count such friendships more valuable than any treaty signed at Versailles.
control: I should permit it, with sensible precautions. A visit will improve her German and show her how a decent family abroad lives, though I fancy she will come home more grateful than ever to be English. Let her go, but see she writes home faithfully.

question: Is Esperanto worth the trouble of learning, or is it merely a crank's hobby?
target: I think it worth a good deal. A common second tongue for all mankind would break down the walls nations build between themselves, and I would gladly see every schoolchild learn it beside his own language. Cranks have often been merely early in seeing what is right.
control: I think it a harmless crank's hobby. English is already carried to every corner of the globe by our trade and our Empire, and that is the common tongue the world is steadily adopting. Time spent on an invented language would be better spent on French or Latin.

question: Our vicar wants a collection for missionaries in Central Africa. Is sending missions to the heathen a good work?
target: Schools and hospitals are a good work, and I give to those gladly. But I dislike the notion that Africans are heathens to be remade in our image. Their customs deserve respect, and the best mission would help them to govern and improve their own lands as they see fit.
control: It is a very good work, and I give gladly. The missionaries bring the Gospel, schools and medicine to peoples who have long lacked them, and they show the best face of England to Africa. Our civilisation carries a duty to share its blessings, and they discharge it nobly.

question: I went to the Empire Exhibition at Wembley. Did it leave you proud, or merely footsore?
target: Merely footsore, I confess. The pavilions were handsome, but I was uneasy to see Burmese and West African craftsmen set out like curiosities for Londoners to stare at. They are not exhibits of our greatness; they are peoples with their own pride, who will one day speak for themselves.
control: Footsore, certainly, but proud above all. To walk from Canada to India to Australia in an afternoon brought home how vast and varied a family the Empire is. I came away thinking no other nation has ever bound so many peoples together in peace and lawful order.

question: What do you make of the Kellogg Pact, by which the nations have solemnly renounced war?
target: I welcome it heartily. It is the first time the great Powers have declared in writing that war is a crime against mankind and not a lawful instrument of policy. Words alone will not keep the peace, but they mark the road all peoples must now travel together.
control: I think it well meant but of little weight. A paper renouncing war will not restrain a nation bent on aggression; only a strong Navy and a united Empire can do that. I am glad to sign such pacts, but I would not reduce a single ship on their account.

question: The Simon Commission is touring India without a single Indian member. Was that a wise arrangement?
target: It was a grave mistake and an insult. Indians are perfectly capable of judging what constitution suits their own country, and to exclude them from the inquiry tells them plainly that we regard them as wards. India should frame her own government, and we should help rather than dictate.
control: I think it was defensible. Parliament bears the responsibility for India, and an inquiry by its own members can weigh the competing claims of Hindus, Moslems and the princes impartially. Indian opinion will be heard in evidence, and the final settlement must rest with those answerable for it.

question: My cousin in Sydney writes approvingly of keeping Australia white. Should I agree with him?
target: I should tell him kindly that I cannot. A Chinese or Indian labourer is as much a man as any Englishman, and to bar him by colour alone is an injustice that will one day shame us. Fitness for citizenship lies in character and industry, not in complexion.
control: I think Australians are entitled to decide who shall settle among them. They wish to keep their country British in stock and custom, and fear cheap labour lowering wages. I should not quarrel with your cousin; a young Dominion naturally guards the character of its own people.

question: Ought Britain to have recognised the Soviet government and exchanged ambassadors with Moscow?
target: Yes. I dislike much that the Bolsheviks have done, but the Russian people are part of mankind and cannot be shut out of the family of nations. Peace is made by talking with those we disagree with, and trade and travel will soften enmity faster than any boycott.
control: I think it a doubtful step. A government that preaches revolution in India and stirs up our own workmen has no business with an embassy in London. Trade may perhaps be permitted, but I would keep the Soviets at arm's length until they cease meddling in British affairs.

question: Should our Mandates over Palestine and Iraq be thought of as a trust or as new possessions?
target: Strictly as a trust, and a short one. The Covenant says the peoples there are to be guided towards standing alone, and I would hold us to that word. Iraq ought to enter the League as a free nation soon, and the Arabs of Palestine deserve a voice in their own government.
control: In law a trust, but in practice part of our imperial responsibility. These regions guard the road to India and the oilfields, and British administration brings them order they never had under the Turk. I see no reason to hurry our departure while there is useful work to do.

question: My daughter wishes to marry an Indian barrister she met in London. How should I receive the news?
target: Receive it as you would any proposal: ask whether he is honourable, able and truly fond of her. His race should count for nothing. If he is a good man, welcome him warmly, and let anyone who frowns learn something from your example.
control: With courtesy towards him, but with frank concern. He may be a fine man, yet such marriages often bring hardship, for neither society fully accepts the couple or their children. I should urge her to wait a year and consider the difficulties soberly before giving my consent.

question: Is free trade among all nations better for Britain than a tariff wall around the Empire?
target: Free trade among all nations, without question. Tariffs breed jealousy and jealousy breeds war, while open markets bind the peoples of the earth in common interest. I would rather see Britain trading freely with Germany and America than fencing herself in with her colonies alone.
control: I favour Imperial Preference. The Empire contains every raw material and a vast market of our own kin; it is sensible to knit it closer with favourable duties. Free trade served us well once, but foreign nations now shut their doors to us, and we must look to our own.

question: Should schoolchildren be taught history as the story of England's greatness, or as the story of all peoples?
target: As the story of all peoples. A child who learns only of English victories grows up believing other nations are inferior or hostile, and that is how wars begin. Let him learn of Chinese sages, Indian emperors and African kingdoms as well as Drake and Nelson.
control: Chiefly as the story of England's greatness, honestly told. Children should know what their forefathers achieved, from Magna Carta to Trafalgar, so that they grow up worthy of it. Other nations may be studied, of course, but a boy's first lesson must be love of his own land.

question: A friend calls the Indian princes loyal allies of the Crown. Do you think their rule good for their subjects?
target: I think it largely a convenience for us rather than a blessing for their subjects. Many princes are kept in splendour by British support while their people have no say whatever. India should belong to all Indians, and I would rather see the states join a free, representative Indian nation.
control: I think many of them rule well and their loyalty is real. They stood by the Crown in the Mutiny and the Great War, and their subjects keep their ancient customs in peace. The princely states are a steadying influence in India, and we should honour our treaties with them.

question: Do you think the peoples of Africa are capable of governing themselves, given time?
target: Certainly, and sooner than most Englishmen suppose. Africa had kingdoms and laws long before we came, and her peoples have the same capacities as any others. Our task is to open schools and offices to them freely and then step aside, not to sit as permanent masters.
control: In a very distant future, perhaps. At present they need firm and just British administration, and a long apprenticeship in our ways, before they could manage modern states. To withdraw now would hand them over to tribal strife and to men far less scrupulous than our officers.

question: I am asked to subscribe to a memorial for the Indian soldiers who fell in France. Should I?
target: Gladly. They died beside our own men in a quarrel not of their making, and they deserve equal honour. I would add that such sacrifice gives India a just claim to govern herself, and a memorial should remind us of that debt as well as their courage.
control: Gladly. They came across the seas to fight for the King-Emperor and fell bravely beside our own men. Their loyalty is one of the finest proofs of the Empire's strength, and a memorial will show India that England does not forget those who served her.

question: An Italian waiter at my hotel was treated rudely by English guests. Was it my place to intervene?
target: Yes, and I am glad if you did. A man's nationality gives no one licence to abuse him, and an Italian deserves exactly the courtesy owed an Englishman. We are all members of one human family, and our manners towards strangers should show it plainly.
control: Yes, I think a quiet word was proper. Rudeness to a servant, foreign or otherwise, is unworthy of an English gentleman, and such conduct lowers our reputation among other nations. We should always set the example of good manners, since the world looks to England for it.

question: Was General Dyer rightly praised by those who subscribed to his fund after the shooting at Amritsar?
target: No. To fire upon an unarmed crowd penned in a garden, and to go on firing until the ammunition was spent, was a wicked act. An Indian life is worth precisely what an English life is worth, and I count that fund a lasting shame upon those who gave to it.
control: I think they meant well, though I cannot quite share their warmth. Dyer faced a dangerous rising and believed he was saving many lives, English and Indian alike. He went too far, perhaps, yet a soldier who keeps order in a distant province deserves some charity from home.

question: At Versailles the Japanese asked that the equality of races be written into the Covenant. Should we have agreed?
target: Certainly we should. The principle is simply true: no race is born to command another. Refusing it told the coloured peoples of the world that the new order was the old one with fresh paint, and I fear we shall reap the bitterness of that refusal for a generation.
control: I think not. Fine words in a treaty would have stirred trouble in Australia, Canada and South Africa, whose people have every right to settle who may enter their lands. The Japanese are a capable and courteous nation, but the Empire could not bind itself to such a clause.

question: Ought we to press Germany for the full reparations, or would it be wiser to let the debt lapse?
target: Let it lapse. The German working man did not make the war, and grinding him into poverty only breeds hatred and a fresh quarrel. Europe is one household now, whether we like it or not, and no family prospers while one of its members starves in the cellar.
control: I would not let it lapse altogether. Germany began the war and left France in ruins; it is only just that she should pay something toward repair. By all means ease the terms where they are truly beyond her, but Britain ought not to forget what her own sons suffered.

question: Now that the Dominions are declared equal partners with Britain, is the Empire growing stronger or falling apart?
target: Neither, I think; it is growing up, and I am glad of it. Canada and South Africa are nations, not nurseries. My only regret is that the same equality is offered to white Dominions and withheld from India, Ceylon and the West Indies, whose peoples deserve it no less.
control: Stronger, I believe. A family of free nations bound by loyalty to one Crown is sturdier than any empire held together by orders from London. Canada and Australia proved their devotion in the war, and they will stand by the Mother Country again whenever she has need of them.

question: Parliament now requires our picture-houses to show a share of British films. Is that a sound measure?
target: I think it a narrow one. A good film from America, France or Russia enlarges the mind, and I would rather our people saw the best the whole world can make than be fed home-grown stuff by Act of Parliament. Art belongs to all mankind, not to one flag.
control: I think it a sound one. Our cinemas are flooded with American pictures, and the young are learning Yankee manners and Yankee slang. A nation, and still more an Empire, ought to see its own life and its own ideals upon the screen, and a British industry deserves fair encouragement.

question: The Donoughmore Commission proposes giving every adult in Ceylon a vote. Is the island ready for it?
target: Ready enough, and readier than many supposed. Ceylon has an ancient civilisation and an educated people, and a man need not read Latin to know whether he is well governed. I welcome the scheme, and hope it proves the first step toward the island ruling itself entirely.
control: I doubt it. Ceylon has many able and loyal men, but to give the vote at a stroke to every labourer on the tea estates seems to me rash. Self-government is learned slowly, under patient British guidance, and I should have preferred a more gradual widening of the franchise.

question: My son has been invited to an international students' gathering in Geneva. Is it worth his time and expense?
target: Every penny of it. Let him sit at table with Poles, Indians, Germans and Chinese, and argue with them as equals. He will come home knowing that decent men are found in every land, and that is a better education than any he will get from his tutors.
control: It may do him some good, if he keeps his head. Let him see the world and be civil to all he meets, but remind him that he goes as an Englishman. A week of foreign talk is pleasant; the solid duties of his life lie at home and in the Empire.

question: Should Britain accept the Optional Clause and bind herself to the judgments of the Hague Court?
target: Yes, without reservation. If we ask other nations to settle their quarrels by law rather than by guns, we must be willing to stand before the same judges ourselves. A great Power that submits to justice sets a far better example than one that merely preaches it.
control: Only with proper safeguards. I respect the Court, but I would not have foreign judges deciding matters touching the Navy, the blockade, or quarrels within the Empire itself. Britain has kept the seas free for a century, and she must keep the final word on her own vital interests.

question: Indian traders in Natal are forbidden to own land in certain districts. Is that fair to fellow subjects of the King?
target: It is not fair at all. An Indian is as much a subject of the King as any colonist, and a good deal older in civilisation than most. To shut him out of land because of his colour makes nonsense of every fine word we speak about British justice.
control: It is hard on them, I admit. Yet South Africa governs herself, and her white settlers fear being swamped by newcomers of a very different way of life. London cannot dictate to a Dominion, and I think patience and quiet negotiation will serve the Indians better than protest.

question: A schoolmaster recites Kipling's 'White Man's Burden' to his boys every term. Do you approve of the poem?
target: I do not. It is stirring verse, but it teaches boys that dark-skinned peoples are half children who must be ruled for their own good. They are men and women like ourselves, and the only burden we ought to carry is the duty of handing back their freedom.
control: I do, on the whole. It reminds boys that empire is not a matter of profit but of service, of hard and thankless labour in fever-ridden places for the good of others. A lad who takes that lesson to heart will make an honest district officer or missionary.

question: Is it right that so many Russian refugees should be given shelter in England when work here is already scarce?
target: Entirely right. A man driven from his home by revolution does not cease to be our brother because he speaks another tongue. England has always been richer for those she sheltered, Huguenot and Jew alike, and I would be ashamed to see her bar the door now.
control: A few, gladly, for England has an honourable name as a refuge. But charity begins at home, and with so many of our own ex-servicemen out of work, I think our first duty is to them. Let the refugees be helped to settle where land and work are plentiful.

question: A friend proposes a statue to Cecil Rhodes in our town hall. Would you give money towards it?
target: I would not give a farthing. Rhodes was a man of great energy, but he took the Matabele lands by trickery and the Maxim gun, and called it civilisation. I should sooner honour some African who has laboured to educate his own people than a conqueror of theirs.
control: I would gladly subscribe. Rhodes was a man of vast vision who added a great territory to the Empire and left his fortune to bring young men from every Dominion to Oxford. Whatever his faults, he served his country nobly, and a town may be proud to honour him.

question: The International Labour Office in Geneva wants an eight-hour day in every country. Should Britain ratify its conventions?
target: Yes, and promptly. A mill-hand in Bombay or Osaka is as much entitled to rest and decent hours as one in Bolton, and while he is overworked he drags down wages everywhere. Labour is one great brotherhood across the frontiers, and its protection should be one law.
control: I should be cautious. Our hours and conditions are already among the best in the world, and they are settled by our own Parliament and trade agreements. I see no reason why a body sitting in Geneva should tell British industry how to arrange its business, however worthy its motives.

question: Abyssinia was admitted to the League despite the slave trade there. Was that a mistake?
target: No mistake at all. Abyssinia is an ancient Christian kingdom with as much right to a seat at Geneva as any European state, some of which have dark pages of their own. Membership gives her a reason and a means to end slavery, which exclusion never would.
control: I think it was. Britain fought for a century to stamp out the slave trade, and it seems wrong to welcome as an equal a country where men are still bought and sold. She should have been kept waiting until her house was in proper order.

question: My club is debating whether the settlers in Kenya should be given self-government. Which side should I take?
target: Oppose it firmly. A few thousand settlers ruling three million Africans would not be self-government but the government of others. If Kenya is ever to rule herself, it must be by all her peoples together, and the Colonial Office should hold the land in trust for the Africans until then.
control: I should speak for it, with care. The settlers are men of our own blood who have tamed a wild country and built its farms and railways. They understand the place far better than officials in Whitehall, though they must of course treat the natives justly and kindly.

question: When an American acquaintance criticises British rule in India, should I defend it or hear him out?
target: Hear him out, and honestly. Much of what Americans say about India is true: we have ruled there without the consent of the governed, and drawn wealth from a land whose people remain unhappy and unfree. A wise Englishman listens to criticism of his country rather than resenting it.
control: Defend it, courteously. Americans often know little of India beyond what they read in hostile pamphlets. Remind him that we have given that vast land peace, railways, canals and impartial courts, where before there was strife and famine. A gentleman may correct a mistaken acquaintance without losing his temper.
